# The DP Pod: The Do Positive Podcast

> **This show turns fresh science and technology results into concrete steps any listener can take today.**
Uploading one clear photo of an insect or plant to a public database can help scientists name new species within weeks.
---
### The Positive Papers
1. **From One Surviving Male Bison, Azerbaijan Now Has 25 Calves Born Wild in 7-Year Success Story: Good News Network**
   Twelve zoo-bred European bison released on the slopes of Shahdagh in northern Azerbaijan in 2019 have now produced 25 calves born in the wild. The project began with a single surviving male and has restored a breeding population on the mountain range. The animals graze and move across the landscape without further human feeding, showing the habitat can support them. Release crates opened seven years ago on the slopes known locally as the Kings Mountain, allowing the herd to encounter an unfamiliar wild setting for the first time. The effort involved coordination with the United Nations and demonstrates that small founding groups can establish self-sustaining numbers when placed in suitable terrain. The result remains limited to one site and one species; wider reintroductions would need similar protected slopes and monitoring. Regular people gain a measurable example that targeted releases can rebuild lost wildlife numbers. Source: [goodnewsnetwork.org](https://www.goodnewsnetwork.org/project-to-return-the-caucasian-bison-sees-sustained-success-after-7-years/)

2. **Acceptor molecule upconverts low-energy green light to high-energy purple with high efficiency: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories**
   A newly designed acceptor molecule converts green light into higher-energy purple light at efficiencies high enough to matter for devices. Solar cells and photocatalysts normally waste longer wavelengths that simply pass through; the upconversion step lets those photons contribute instead. The work comes from laboratory measurements reported this week. The molecule has not yet been tested inside full commercial panels, so real-world durability and cost remain unknown. Researchers focused on an acceptor structure that pairs with a donor to shift photon energy upward, capturing green wavelengths that standard materials ignore. Early lab results indicate the process operates without requiring extreme conditions or rare materials. Listeners see a path toward future panels that could use more of the sunlight that reaches rooftops. Source: [phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-acceptor-molecule-upconverts-energy-green.html)

3. **Scrolling for science: How a Twitter post discovered a new wasp in Fukuoka, Japan: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories**
   Several people posted photos of an unfamiliar wasp online; experts later identified it as the previously unknown species Eupelmus curvator. The find shows that ordinary nature photographs can supply the first records of new insects when shared publicly. The process relies on existing free platforms and expert review rather than new equipment. Observers in Fukuoka captured images that circulated on social media and drew specialist attention within days. Scale is still small—most posts do not yield new species—but the barrier to entry is only a phone camera and an upload. The discovery illustrates how distributed observations can accelerate taxonomy without dedicated field expeditions. Source: [phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-scrolling-science-twitter-wasp-fukuoka.html)
---
### The Lever
Take a clear photo of any insect, plant, or bird you notice today and upload it to a free citizen-science app such as iNaturalist. The action takes under two minutes once the app is installed. Each verified observation adds one data point to maps used by researchers; the wasp discovery shows a single post can trigger a formal species description. If even one percent of regular listeners added one observation per week, the total would reach thousands of new records each month, enough to fill gaps in regional biodiversity surveys. The main barrier is not knowing the platforms exist; downloading the app and following its two-tap upload flow removes it. Observations remain useful even without species identification because algorithms and later expert review can refine the record over time. The approach works at any scale because each upload stands alone yet contributes to cumulative datasets that track distribution changes. Source: [phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-scrolling-science-twitter-wasp-fukuoka.html)
---
### Do Positive Dispatch
No dispatches in the bag today — try the photo-upload step above and report what you spotted.
---
